title: Chemical Reactions: Reactants, Products and Evidence
kicker: Cambridge Primary Checkpoint · Science 0097 · Stage 6 · Chemistry
summary: What a chemical reaction is, how to name reactants and products in a word equation, and the three pieces of evidence Checkpoint asks about: a gas being produced, a change in colour and a change in temperature.

blocks.title: In the curriculum
items: Understand that in a chemical reaction, substances called reactants interact (react) to make new substances called products. (6Cc.04)
Observe and describe the evidence that a chemical reaction has happened: a gas is produced, the colour changes, or the temperature changes. (6Cc.05)

blocks.text: 1. Key words

items: chemical reaction
تفاعل كيميائي — a change in which new substances are made
reactants
المتفاعلات — the substances you start with, before the reaction
products
النواتج — the new substances made by the reaction
word equation
معادلة لفظية — reactants → products, written in words
evidence
دليل — something you observe that shows a reaction has happened
fizzing / effervescence
فوران — many bubbles of gas being produced
irreversible
غير عكسي — cannot be changed back to the starting substances
acid
حمض — e.g. vinegar or lemon juice; reacts with some substances (wear goggles)

blocks.text: 2. What is a chemical reaction?

In a physical change (melting, dissolving, boiling) the substance stays the same substance. In a **chemical reaction**, the starting substances **react** — their particles join up in a new way — and **new substances** are made. The new substances have different properties from the old ones.

items: **Reactants** = the substances at the start (the ones that are used up).
**Products** = the new substances made at the end.
Most chemical reactions are **irreversible**: you cannot easily get the reactants back. A burnt match cannot become a match again; a cooked egg cannot be uncooked.

blocks.text: 3. Writing a word equation

We show a reaction with a **word equation**. The reactants go on the **left**, the products on the **right**, and the arrow means "react to make". A plus sign (+) separates substances. **Never use an equals sign.**

rows: carbon dioxide + water + a new salt

blocks.text: **Oxygen** from the air is a reactant in burning and rusting, even though you cannot see it. That is why a candle under a jar goes out, and why a nail kept in dry air with no oxygen and no water does not rust.

blocks.title: Reading a word equation
blocks.text: Everything **before** the arrow = reactants. Everything **after** the arrow = products. If a question asks "name one product", choose any one substance after the arrow — not the whole side.
4. Evidence of a chemical reaction
We cannot see particles, so we look for clues. At Stage 6 you must know three kinds of evidence:

rows: bubbles, fizzing, a balloon on the flask fills up
baking soda + vinegar; chalk + vinegar; magnesium + acid; baking powder making a cake rise
the colour of the substance is different afterwards
grey iron → orange-brown rust; white bread → brown toast; a cut apple turns brown; a copper roof slowly turns green; clear egg white → white when cooked
the mixture gets hotter (or colder) — measure with a thermometer
burning gives out heat; magnesium + acid gets warmer; air-activated hand warmers (iron powder reacting with oxygen) get hot; baking soda + vinegar gets colder

blocks.text: **Temperature change:** put a thermometer in the reactants, read it before mixing, then read it again after the reaction. Temperature change = higher reading − lower reading. Say whether it went **up** (got hotter) or **down** (got colder) — both are evidence.

blocks.title: Careful — physical changes can look similar
items: Boiling water makes bubbles, but the gas is still water (water vapour) — no new substance, so it is not a reaction.
Heating water makes it hotter, but nothing new is made.
Mixing blue and yellow paint makes green, but the paints are only mixed.
Bubbles from a fizzy drink are gas that was already dissolved in it.
So the evidence is a clue. The real test is: **has a new substance been made?**

blocks.title: تذكر
blocks.text: التفاعل الكيميائي = مواد جديدة تتكون. المواد في البداية اسمها reactants (المتفاعلات) وتُكتب قبل السهم، والمواد الجديدة اسمها products (النواتج) وتُكتب بعد السهم. الأدلة المطلوبة ثلاثة فقط: خروج غاز (فقاعات/فوران)، تغير اللون، تغير درجة الحرارة (سخونة أو برودة).
5. Physical change or chemical reaction?

rows: ice melting, salt dissolving, water boiling, wax melting
wax burning, bread toasting, iron rusting, milk going sour
change of state or shape; the substance is still the same
gas made, colour change, temperature change

blocks.text: A candle is a good example of both. The wax near the flame **melts** (physical, reversible: it sets again when it cools). The wax vapour in the flame **burns** (chemical: wax + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water), giving out heat and light.
6. Chemical reactions in everyday life

items: **Cooking:** frying an egg, toasting bread and grilling meat all make new substances (the colour change shows this).
**Baking:** baking powder reacts in the hot, wet cake mixture and makes carbon dioxide gas; the bubbles make the cake rise.
**Burning fuels:** natural gas in a cooker, petrol in a car and wood on a fire react with oxygen and give out heat.
**Rusting:** iron on bridges, cars and railings reacts with oxygen and water. Painting or oiling iron keeps the water and oxygen away.
**Food going bad:** milk going sour and fruit going brown are slow reactions.

blocks.caption: A rusty iron chain: iron reacted with oxygen and water to make orange-brown rust, a new substance.

blocks.text: 7. Gases have mass too

When a reaction makes a gas in an **open** flask, the gas escapes into the air and the balance reading goes **down**. The gas has mass, and it has left the flask. If a balloon (or a stopper) traps the gas, the reading stays the same, because nothing has left. Mass lost = starting mass − final mass.
8. Worked examples
**Worked example 1** — Look at the word equation: **magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide**. (a) Name the two reactants. [1] (b) Name the product. [1] (c) Why is this a chemical reaction? [1]

items: (a) The reactants are before the arrow: **magnesium and oxygen**.
(b) The product is after the arrow: **magnesium oxide**.
(c) A **new substance** (magnesium oxide) is made.
**Common mistake:** writing "magnesium oxide" as a reactant because it contains the word magnesium. Look at which side of the arrow it is on.

blocks.text: **Worked example 2** — Yara adds iron filings to blue copper sulfate solution. After a few minutes the solution turns pale green, a brown-red solid forms on the iron, and the thermometer reading rises from 21 °C to 26 °C. Give **two** pieces of evidence that a chemical reaction happened. [2 marks]

items: The colour changed (blue → pale green, and a red-brown solid appeared) (1).
The temperature rose by 5 °C (26 − 21 = 5) (1).
**Exam tip:** describe what you **see** ("the solution turned from blue to green"), not just "it changed".

blocks.text: **Worked example 3** — Before Ziad mixes baking soda and vinegar the thermometer reads 21 °C. After mixing it reads 16 °C. (a) Calculate the temperature change. [1] (b) Is this evidence of a chemical reaction? Explain. [1]

items: (a) 21 − 16 = **5 °C** (a **fall** of 5 °C — the mixture got colder).
(b) Yes — a change in temperature is evidence of a reaction; it can be a rise **or** a fall. (The fizzing, a gas being produced, is more evidence.)
**Common mistake:** thinking only "getting hotter" counts.

blocks.text: **Worked example 4** — A flask of vinegar and chalk has a mass of 210.0 g at the start. When the fizzing stops, the mass is 207.8 g. The flask was open. (a) Calculate the mass lost. [1] (b) Explain why the mass went down. [1]

items: (b) A gas (carbon dioxide) was produced and **escaped** into the air from the open flask; the gas has mass, so the flask lost mass.
**Common mistake:** "the mass was destroyed" or "gas has no mass". Gases do have mass.

blocks.text: **Worked example 5** — Ahmed heats water in a kettle. It bubbles and gets hot. He says: "This is a chemical reaction because there are bubbles and a temperature change." Is he right? Explain. [2 marks]

items: No, he is not right (1).
No new substance is made — the bubbles are water vapour, which is still water; it can condense back into liquid water. Boiling is a physical (reversible) change (1).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
items: Mixing up reactants (start, left of the arrow) and products (end, right of the arrow).
Using "=" in a word equation instead of "→".
Forgetting **oxygen** as a reactant in burning and rusting.
Saying "it changed" — always describe the evidence: what gas/bubbles, which colours (from → to), how much the temperature rose or fell.
Thinking a fall in temperature is not evidence — getting colder counts too.
Calling boiling, melting or dissolving "reactions" — they make no new substance.

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks this
items: **Name the reactants / products** from a word equation, or **complete** a word equation with a missing word.
**What is the evidence?** — from a description, picture or results table: bubbles/gas, colour change, temperature change.
**Read two thermometers** and work out the change — show the subtraction and write °C.
**Change in mass** — subtract and explain that a gas escaped.
**Tick the chemical reactions** in a list — look for new substances (burning, cooking, rusting, baking).
**Safety** — wear eye protection with acids; never taste chemicals.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Chemical reactions — practice
blocks.intro: Answer every part. Type short answers in the box; for longer answers write yours on paper, then mark it with the mark scheme.

questions.q: What name is given to the substances at the start of a chemical reaction?
questions.e: The starting substances are the reactants. The new substances made are the products.

questions.q: Which is the product of this reaction?
questions.e: The product is written after the arrow: magnesium oxide. Magnesium and oxygen are the reactants.

questions.q: Which observation shows that a chemical reaction is happening?
c: sugar disappearing when it is stirred into water
an ice cube melting on a plate
water bubbling in a hot pan
bubbles of a new gas when chalk is put in vinegar
questions.e: Chalk and vinegar react to make a new gas (carbon dioxide). Dissolving, melting and boiling are physical changes — no new substance is made.

questions.p:
Question 4
Salma puts a thermometer in some dilute acid. Then she adds a piece of magnesium ribbon. The thermometers show the temperature before and after the reaction.
questions.q: By how many degrees did the temperature change?
questions.e: Each small division is 1 °C. Before: 19 °C; after: 27 °C. Change = 27 − 19 = 8 °C (a rise). A temperature change is evidence of a chemical reaction.

questions.q: Baking soda reacts with vinegar and the mixture fizzes. Name the gas that is produced.
questions.e: The gas is carbon dioxide. It is the same gas that makes a cake rise when baking powder reacts in the oven.

questions.q: Describe three different kinds of evidence that a chemical reaction has taken place.
questions.ms: 1 mark each: a gas is produced / bubbles / fizzing; a change in colour; a change in temperature (gets hotter or colder). Ignore: "it changes" without saying what. Note: give credit for clear examples of each type, e.g. "the balloon fills with gas". Also accept other correct signs of a new substance, e.g. light or a flame given out, a new solid appearing, a new smell.
questions.e: (1) A gas is produced — you see bubbles or fizzing. (2) The colour changes — e.g. grey iron turns orange-brown. (3) The temperature changes — the mixture gets hotter or colder.

questions.p:
Question 7
Nadia puts a flask of vinegar on a balance. She adds some baking soda, and the mixture fizzes. She does not put a lid or balloon on the flask.
Mass of flask and contents just after adding the baking soda: 150.0 g. Mass when the fizzing stops: 148.5 g.
questions.q: (a) Calculate the mass that was lost.

questions.p:
Question 7
Nadia puts a flask of vinegar on a balance. She adds some baking soda, and the mixture fizzes. She does not put a lid or balloon on the flask.
Mass of flask and contents just after adding the baking soda: 150.0 g. Mass when the fizzing stops: 148.5 g.
questions.q: (b) Explain why the mass of the flask went down.
questions.ms: 1 mark: a gas (carbon dioxide) was made and escaped (from the open flask) — gas has mass. Do not accept: the mass was destroyed / the liquid evaporated.
questions.e: The reaction made carbon dioxide gas. The flask was open, so the gas escaped into the air. Gases have mass, so the flask lost mass.

questions.p:
Question 7
Nadia puts a flask of vinegar on a balance. She adds some baking soda, and the mixture fizzes. She does not put a lid or balloon on the flask.
Mass of flask and contents just after adding the baking soda: 150.0 g. Mass when the fizzing stops: 148.5 g.
questions.q: (c) Nadia repeats the experiment with a balloon over the top of the flask to trap all of the gas. The mass at the start is 150.0 g. What will the mass be when the fizzing stops?
questions.e: The balloon traps the gas, so nothing leaves the flask. The mass stays at 150.0 g.

questions.q: An iron nail is left outside in the rain for a month. What evidence shows that a chemical reaction has happened?
c: a change in colour from grey to orange-brown
bubbles of gas coming off the nail
questions.e: Iron reacts with oxygen and water to make rust, which is orange-brown. Getting wet is not a reaction, and rusting is too slow to make the nail feel hot or to see bubbles.

questions.q: Name the product of this reaction.
questions.e: The product is after the arrow: rust (a type of iron oxide). Iron, oxygen and water are the reactants.

questions.q: Which of these is a chemical reaction?
questions.e: Burning makes new substances (ash, carbon dioxide and water) and gives out heat and light; it cannot be reversed. The other three are physical changes.

questions.q: Omar says: "Boiling water makes bubbles, so boiling is a chemical reaction." Explain why Omar is wrong.
questions.ms: 1 mark: no new substance is made / the bubbles are water vapour (still water). 1 mark: boiling is a physical / reversible change — the vapour can condense back to water. Accept: bubbles alone do not prove a reaction.
questions.e: The bubbles in boiling water are water vapour, which is still water, so no new substance is made. Boiling is a physical change: cooling the vapour turns it back into liquid water. Bubbles are only evidence of a reaction if a new gas is made.

questions.q: A cut apple is left on a plate for one hour. Describe the evidence that a chemical reaction has happened.
questions.ms: 1 mark: the colour changes — the cut surface turns (from white/cream) to brown. Do not accept: it goes bad / it dries.
questions.e: The cut surface of the apple changes colour from white (cream) to brown. Substances in the apple react with oxygen in the air to make new, brown substances.

blocks.title: Remember
items: Chemical reaction = new substances are made; usually irreversible.
Reactants (start) → products (new). Word equations use + and →, never =.
Evidence at Stage 6: a gas is produced (bubbles/fizzing), a colour change, a temperature change (up or down).
Bubbles or heating alone are not proof: ask whether a new substance was made.
In an open flask the gas escapes, so the mass goes down — gases have mass.
